content: 1. Effective Surveillance and Data Management Systems: Patients with leprosy are mapped at sub-national levels and linked to health facilities. Data is digitized and managed through web-based systems, enabling analysis for planning the Zero Leprosy Roadmap. Data management is synchronized with drug requests and supply systems. A case-based data management system is implemented for all cases, ensuring comprehensive surveillance. 2. Contact Tracing: Contacts of all new leprosy cases and cases detected in the past five years are listed and screened. Counseling is provided to obtain consent for contact examinations. Neighbors and social contacts are screened annually for five years. Contacts of non-autochthonous cases are mapped for local screening or, if feasible, in the source country. Confirmed cases among contacts are documented, and the coverage of contact tracing is monitored. 3. Rifampicin is made available for prophylactic use. Household and social contacts are screened, and single-dose rifampicin (SDR) chemoprophylaxis is administered to eligible contacts. Preventive chemotherapy is provided to the maximum number of eligible contacts. 4. Documentation at Sub-National and National Levels: Sub-national units prepare documentation similar to a dossier for internal review. A country dossier is prepared and submitted when claiming leprosy elimination. 5. Leprosy Transmission Assessment Survey (LTAS): Health facilities are assessed, and data is reviewed to evaluate the epidemiological situation. The goal is to achieve zero autochthonous child cases for five consecutive years. Health facilities are aligned with referral systems and standard operating procedures (SOPs). 6. Monitoring, Evaluation, and Verification: Internal evaluations assess the interruption of transmission through LTAS at sub-national levels. Mechanisms are established for continued monitoring of leprosy cases and trends. Dossiers are submitted for verification by the World Health Organization (WHO). Systems are in place to retrieve and compare data annually to track progress. 7. Phase 3: Sustaining Elimination: Once a country achieves zero autochthonous child cases for five consecutive years, it must sustain this status to move toward disease elimination. Disease elimination is defined as zero autochthonous cases for three years or until transmission interruption is declared. Countries fulfilling these criteria can claim disease elimination, even if sporadic cases occur. 8. Phase 4: Post-Elimination Phase: Post-elimination surveillance is included in the national health plan for ten years in areas where elimination is achieved. Surveillance is conducted through sentinel or referral centers and apex health centers. SOPs are developed for leprosy surveillance, and trained staff are allocated to maintain quality services. 9. Research and Innovations: Research focuses on innovations to reach refugees, migrants, and displaced populations. Data from sub-national levels are analyzed to review trends and verify progress toward elimination. 10. Country-Specific Examples: In Brazil, data from municipalities showed a significant reduction in new cases, particularly among children, indicating reduced transmission. In Tamil Nadu, India, active case detection in high-endemic blocks revealed the necessity of continued active search in endemic areas. In the Maldives, many islands achieved elimination benchmarks, with sporadic cases not reversing elimination status. In Morocco, most regions achieved transmission interruption, with a few provinces still working toward elimination. 11. Global Application: Data from countries like Thailand and Vietnam demonstrate progress toward transmission interruption and elimination. Maps indicate regions achieving elimination milestones, with post-elimination surveillance ensuring sustained progress. This detailed approach highlights the importance of robust surveillance, targeted interventions, and sustained efforts to achieve and maintain leprosy elimination globally.
